content: Gonorrhea is a significant cause of severe reproductive complications in women, including pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility. It also facilitates the transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). In the United States, gonorrhea is the second most commonly reported notifiable infection, with over 300,000 cases reported in 2011. The treatment of gonorrhea has become increasingly challenging due to the ability of Neisseria gonorrhoeae to develop resistance to antimicrobials. During the 1990s and 2000s, resistance to fluoroquinolones emerged in the United States, initially in Hawaii, California, and among men who have sex with men (MSM), before spreading nationwide. By 2007, the prevalence of fluoroquinolone-resistant N. gonorrhoeae led the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to stop recommending fluoroquinolones for gonorrhea treatment, leaving cephalosporins as the only remaining recommended antimicrobial class. The CDC's Gonococcal Isolate Surveillance Project (GISP) has monitored N. gonorrhoeae antimicrobial susceptibilities since 1986. Data from GISP between 2006 and 2011 revealed declining susceptibility to cefixime among urethral N. gonorrhoeae isolates in the United States. Reports from Europe have also documented cases of uncomplicated gonorrhea that were not cured by cefixime 400 mg orally. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of cefixime is waning. In response, the CDC updated its treatment guidelines. For uncomplicated gonorrhea infections of the cervix, urethra, rectum, or pharynx, the CDC recommends combination therapy with a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone 250 mg plus either a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g or oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. Cefixime is no longer recommended as a first-line treatment. If cefixime is used as an alternative, a test-of-cure should be performed one week after treatment. For patients with severe cephalosporin allergies, azithromycin 2 g orally in a single dose is recommended, along with a test-of-cure. Ceftriaxone is highly effective against N. gonorrhoeae infections at all anatomic sites and provides sustained bactericidal levels in the blood. However, clinical data supporting doses of ceftriaxone higher than 250 mg are limited. Cefixime, in contrast, does not achieve the same bactericidal levels or sustained efficacy, particularly for pharyngeal gonorrhea. The emergence of N. gonorrhoeae strains with elevated cefixime minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs), particularly in the western United States and among MSM, is concerning. This pattern mirrors the early stages of fluoroquinolone resistance development in the 1990s. Rising cefixime MICs are expected to lead to declining cefixime effectiveness for urogenital gonorrhea treatment. Continued use of cefixime may accelerate the development of resistance to ceftriaxone, the last highly effective single-dose treatment for gonorrhea. To preserve ceftriaxone's effectiveness, the CDC no longer recommends routine use of cefixime as a first-line treatment. Combination therapy with two antimicrobials with different mechanisms of action is recommended to improve treatment efficacy and delay the emergence of resistance. Azithromycin is preferred as the second antimicrobial due to its single-dose convenience and lower prevalence of resistance compared to doxycycline. Clinicians diagnosing gonorrhea in patients with persistent infection after recommended combination therapy should perform culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing of N. gonorrhoeae isolates. Phenotypic susceptibility testing should be conducted using disk diffusion, Etest, or agar dilution methods. If treatment failure occurs, patients should be treated with ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly and azithromycin 2 g orally, and infectious disease consultation should be sought. Cases of treatment failure should be reported to the CDC within 24 hours of diagnosis. Efforts must be made to ensure that patients' sexual partners from the preceding 60 days are evaluated and treated promptly. If partners cannot be linked to care, expedited partner therapy with oral combination antimicrobials (cefixime 400 mg and azithromycin 1 g) should be considered. The capacity of U.S. laboratories to isolate N. gonorrhoeae by culture is declining due to the widespread use of nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for diagnosis. However, maintaining culture capacity is essential for monitoring antimicrobial resistance trends and guiding treatment following treatment failure. Health-care providers must retain the ability to collect specimens for culture and be aware of laboratories capable of performing culture. Health-care systems and health departments must support access to culture, and laboratories must maintain or develop partnerships to ensure culture capacity. Effective treatment of gonorrhea with the most reliable therapies will limit transmission, prevent complications, and likely slow the emergence of resistance. However, resistance to cephalosporins, including ceftriaxone, is anticipated. Reinvestment in gonorrhea prevention and control is warranted, and new treatment options are urgently needed.
